Topical to oral mucosa; not related to meals (avoid eating immediately after applying)
Avoid, especially third trimester (salicylate effects on fetus/closure of ductus)
Salicylates can pass into milk; avoid or use with caution

summary: Choline salicylate is a water-soluble, non-acetylated salicylate used chiefly as an oromucosal gel for the relief of pain from mouth ulcers, denture irritation and teething. Applied topically it provides local analgesic and anti-inflammatory relief. Because it is a salicylate it should be avoided in children and adolescents with febrile viral illnesses (risk of Reye syndrome) and used cautiously in salicylate-sensitive or peptic-ulcer patients. Note: choline salicylate is not an FDA-approved product in the US; the information below is based on EMA/SmPC and BNF sources.
indications: Symptomatic relief of pain from mouth ulcers (aphthous ulcers)
Relief of soreness from dentures and orthodontic appliances
Relief of teething pain (in formulations and age groups where permitted)

dosage.d: Apply about 1 cm of gel with a clean finger, massage gently
dosage.t: Not more often than every 3 hours

dosage.d: Apply small amount to the affected gum
dosage.n: Follow age restrictions on the specific product; many labels now restrict in young children

dosage.c: Ear use (choline salicylate ear drops, where marketed)
dosage.d: Instill drops into the affected ear as directed
dosage.n: For softening earwax / otitis externa per product label

admin: Apply the gel directly to the painful area with a clean fingertip and massage gently
Avoid eating or drinking for a short time after application to keep the gel in contact
Do not exceed the stated frequency (no more often than every 3 hours)
Do not apply to large areas or use for prolonged periods due to salicylate absorption
Avoid in children/adolescents with chickenpox, influenza or other febrile viral illness (Reye syndrome risk)
moa: Choline salicylate is a salicylate that inhibits cyclo-oxygenase, reducing prostaglandin synthesis at the site of application and thereby producing local analgesic and anti-inflammatory effects on inflamed oral mucosa. Unlike aspirin it is non-acetylated, giving relatively weak irreversible platelet effects.

absolute: Children and adolescents with febrile viral illness (Reye syndrome risk) - per product restrictions
Active peptic ulceration (for systemic salicylate exposure)
relative: Use in young infants (many labels restrict by age)
monitor: Signs of salicylate excess if overused (tinnitus, GI upset)

preg: Avoid, particularly in the third trimester. Salicylates cross the placenta and, with significant exposure, can affect fetal circulation (premature closure of the ductus arteriosus) and increase bleeding risk. Limited topical oral use is lower risk but should be avoided where possible.
lact: Salicylates are excreted into breast milk. Avoid or use with caution during breastfeeding because of the theoretical risk of adverse effects (including Reye syndrome) in the infant.
renal: Use with caution in renal impairment. Although topical oral use gives low systemic exposure, excessive or prolonged application can lead to salicylate accumulation.
hepatic: Use with caution in hepatic impairment. Avoid in children and adolescents with viral illness because of the association of salicylates with Reye syndrome (hepatic and CNS injury).

major: Other salicylates / aspirin (additive salicylate effect and toxicity if overused)
Anticoagulants e.g. warfarin (salicylates increase bleeding risk)
Methotrexate (salicylates reduce its clearance - relevant with substantial absorption)
interactions.food: Avoid eating/drinking immediately after application to prolong local contact
interactions.alcohol: Avoid excessive alcohol - additive gastrointestinal irritation with systemic salicylate
interactions.diagnostics: Heavy use may register measurable serum salicylate; can affect some urine glucose tests

common: Transient local stinging or burning at the application site
serious: Hypersensitivity / salicylate allergic reactions including bronchospasm
Mucosal ulceration with excessive or prolonged use
Salicylate toxicity if grossly overused (especially in children)
emergency: Features of salicylate poisoning (hyperventilation, vomiting, tinnitus, confusion)

monitoring: Watch for excessive/prolonged use, especially in children
counsel: Apply a small amount only to the sore area with a clean finger
Do not use more often than every 3 hours
Do not eat or drink straight after applying
Do not give salicylate products to children with chickenpox or flu-like illness unless advised
See a doctor or dentist if mouth ulcers last more than about 3 weeks
pk: Local pain relief within minutes of application
Local effect develops shortly after application
Systemic salicylate half-life ~2-3 hours at low doses (dose-dependent); minimal with topical use
Local effect lasts roughly 2-3 hours, hence repeat dosing
Store below 25 C; keep the tube tightly closed and out of reach of children
pearls: Not FDA-approved; guidance here is based on EMA/SmPC and BNF
Being a salicylate, it should be avoided in children with febrile viral illnesses (Reye syndrome) - several regulators restrict use under defined ages
Useful as an alcohol-free, sugar-free local oral analgesic alternative to benzocaine gels
Limit area and duration of application to minimise systemic salicylate absorption
Persistent or non-healing mouth ulcers warrant evaluation to exclude serious pathology
missed: This is a when-required topical medicine, so there is no fixed schedule - simply apply when symptoms need relief, respecting the minimum 3-hour interval and the maximum applications per day. Do not apply extra to make up for a missed application.
overdose: Topical overuse, or accidental ingestion (especially by children), can cause salicylate poisoning: nausea, vomiting, tinnitus, hyperventilation, sweating, and in severe cases acid-base disturbance, seizures and coma. Stop the product and seek urgent medical help; management is supportive with attention to fluids, electrolytes and acid-base, urinary alkalinisation, and dialysis in severe poisoning.
